topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Chemical Bonds
topics.description: An overview of the three main types of strong chemical bond — ionic, covalent and metallic — and why atoms bond together.
learning_objectives: State why atoms form chemical bonds
Name the three main types of strong chemical bond
Identify which type of bond is likely to form between given elements
topics.explanation: A chemical bond is a strong force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together in a compound or element, formed as atoms interact to achieve a more stable, lower-energy electron arrangement (usually a full outer shell, following the octet rule). There are three main types of strong chemical bond: ionic bonding, the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal; covalent bonding, formed when two non-metal atoms share one or more pairs of electrons; and metallic bonding, formed between metal atoms, involving a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised electrons. Which type of bond forms depends largely on the elements involved: metal + non-metal typically gives ionic bonding; non-metal + non-metal typically gives covalent bonding; metal + metal gives metallic bonding.
key_concepts: Predicting bond type from element combination

definitions.definition: A strong force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together, formed to achieve a more stable electron arrangement.

worked_examples.problem: Predict the type of bonding expected between magnesium and oxygen.
worked_examples.working: Magnesium is a metal; oxygen is a non-metal.
worked_examples.answer: Ionic bonding is expected, since a metal reacting with a non-metal typically involves electron transfer to form ions.

practical_applications: Understanding bond type is essential for predicting a substance's physical properties (melting point, conductivity, solubility) in materials science and industrial chemistry
common_mistakes: Assuming all bonds between different elements are automatically ionic — bonding type depends on whether both elements are metals, both non-metals, or one of each
misconceptions: Believing bonding always follows a strict either/or categorisation — bonding actually exists on a spectrum, with many bonds showing a mixture of ionic and covalent character depending on the electronegativity difference involved
tips: Use a simple rule of thumb: metal + non-metal → ionic; non-metal + non-metal → covalent; metal + metal → metallic

basic.question: Name the three main types of strong chemical bond.
State the type of bonding expected between two chlorine atoms.

intermediate.question: Explain, in general terms, why atoms form chemical bonds.
intermediate.answer: Atoms form chemical bonds to achieve a more stable, lower-energy electron arrangement, usually by gaining a full outer shell of electrons (the octet rule, or 2 electrons for hydrogen/helium), which is achieved through losing, gaining, or sharing electrons with other atoms.

advanced.question: Explain why the bonding in a compound like aluminium chloride can be considered to have significant covalent character, despite aluminium being a metal and chlorine a non-metal.
advanced.answer: Although the simple metal + non-metal rule suggests ionic bonding, the actual bond character depends on the electronegativity difference and the polarising power of the cation involved. Aluminium ions (Al3+) are small and highly charged, giving them strong polarising power, which distorts the electron cloud of the neighbouring chloride ions significantly, pulling electron density towards the aluminium and giving the bond substantial covalent character rather than being purely ionic, illustrating that the simple ionic/covalent/metallic categorisation is a simplification of a more continuous spectrum of bonding character.

exam_style_questions.question: Predict and justify the type of bonding present in (a) sodium chloride, (b) carbon dioxide, and (c) copper metal.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: (a) Ionic bonding, since sodium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal, so electrons are transferred to form ions (1 mark). (b) Covalent bonding, since carbon and oxygen are both non-metals, so electrons are shared (1 mark). (c) Metallic bonding, since copper is a metal, involving a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons (1 mark).

topics.summary: Chemical bonds are strong attractive forces formed as atoms achieve a more stable electron arrangement. The three main types are ionic (metal + non-metal, electron transfer), covalent (non-metal + non-metal, electron sharing), and metallic (metal + metal, delocalised electrons).
revision_notes: Metal + non-metal → ionic
Non-metal + non-metal → covalent
Metal + metal → metallic
All bonding aims for a stable, full outer shell

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Ionic Bonding
topics.description: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.
learning_objectives: Define ionic bonding
Describe the process of electron transfer in ionic bond formation
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams to represent ionic bond formation
topics.explanation: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when one or more electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. The metal atom loses electrons to form a positively charged cation, while the non-metal atom gains those electrons to form a negatively charged anion; both ions typically achieve a full, stable outer shell (matching the nearest noble gas configuration) as a result. The oppositely charged ions are then held together by strong electrostatic attraction, extending in all directions to form a giant ionic lattice (see Ionic Lattices). Ionic bonding is typically represented using dot-and-cross diagrams, which show the transfer of electrons explicitly, with dots representing electrons from one atom and crosses representing electrons from the other, to make clear which atom each electron originated from.
key_concepts: Electron transfer from metal to non-metal

definitions.definition: The strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.

worked_examples.problem: Describe the formation of an ionic bond between magnesium and oxygen.
worked_examples.working: Magnesium (2,8,2) has 2 valence electrons; oxygen (2,6) needs 2 more electrons to complete its outer shell. Magnesium transfers both its outer electrons to oxygen.
worked_examples.answer: Magnesium loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+ (2,8); oxygen gains 2 electrons to form O2− (2,8). The oppositely charged Mg2+ and O2− ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction, forming magnesium oxide, MgO.

practical_applications: Ionic bonding explains the high melting points and electrical behaviour of salts, essential to processes such as electrolysis and the manufacture of ceramics
common_mistakes: Drawing dot-and-cross diagrams that show electron sharing (like covalent bonding) rather than complete electron transfer for ionic compounds
misconceptions: Believing ionic bonding only involves a single pair of ions — the electrostatic attraction extends in all directions throughout a giant lattice structure, not just between one pair of ions
tips: When drawing ionic dot-and-cross diagrams, always show square brackets around each ion with the charge written outside the top right corner

basic.question: Define ionic bonding.
basic.answer: The strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.

basic.question: State which type of atom (metal or non-metal) typically loses electrons in ionic bonding.

intermediate.question: Describe, with reference to electron transfer, how an ionic bond forms between potassium and chlorine.
intermediate.answer: A potassium atom (electron configuration 2,8,8,1) transfers its single outer-shell electron to a chlorine atom (electron configuration 2,8,7). This gives potassium a full outer shell, forming K+ (2,8,8), and gives chlorine a full outer shell, forming Cl− (2,8,8). The oppositely charged K+ and Cl− ions are then held together by strong electrostatic attraction, forming potassium chloride, KCl.

intermediate.question: Explain why sodium forms a 1+ ion rather than losing more than one electron when bonding ionically.
intermediate.answer: Sodium has only one valence (outer-shell) electron; losing this single electron gives sodium a full, stable outer shell matching the electron configuration of neon. Losing any further electrons would require removing electrons from a full inner shell, which requires vastly more energy and is not energetically favourable, so sodium consistently forms only a 1+ ion.

advanced.question: Explain why ionic bonding results in a giant lattice structure rather than discrete pairs of ions.
advanced.answer: Once ions form, their electrostatic attraction is non-directional (acting equally in all directions around each ion, unlike the directional sharing of electrons in covalent bonding) and each ion attracts multiple oppositely charged ions around it, not just one. This mutual attraction between many ions extends throughout the structure, with each ion surrounded by several oppositely charged neighbours arranged in a strict, repeating, three-dimensional pattern that minimises overall energy (by maximising attraction between opposite charges and minimising repulsion between like charges), producing a giant ionic lattice rather than isolated ion pairs.

exam_style_questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram (describe in words) to show the formation of calcium chloride, CaCl2, from calcium and chlorine atoms.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: A calcium atom (2,8,8,2) transfers one electron to each of two separate chlorine atoms (2,8,7) (1 mark). This gives calcium a full outer shell, forming Ca2+ (2,8,8), and gives each chlorine a full outer shell, forming two separate Cl− ions (2,8,8) (1 mark). The diagram would show [Ca]2+ with two separate [Cl]− ions, each with 8 electrons shown around it (one originally a cross from calcium), demonstrating the 1:2 ratio of calcium to chloride ions in CaCl2 (1 mark).

topics.summary: Ionic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons transfer from a metal to a non-metal, both achieving stable, full outer shells. This attraction extends throughout a giant lattice structure.
revision_notes: Ionic bonding: electron transfer, metal → non-metal
Both ions achieve full outer shell (noble gas configuration)
Attraction is non-directional, extends throughout a giant lattice
Represented using dot-and-cross diagrams with square brackets and charges
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Dot-and-cross diagram showing electron transfer from sodium to chlorine forming Na+ and Cl-]

images.description: A two-panel diagram showing a sodium atom with its single outer electron highlighted and an arrow indicating transfer to a chlorine atom (shown with its seven outer electrons), followed by the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions with appropriate charges, and summary text stating 'Na loses 1 electron -> Na+; Cl gains 1 electron -> Cl-'.
images.purpose: Makes the abstract process of electron transfer in ionic bonding concrete and visual, directly illustrating the worked example given in the text.
images.placement: After the worked example, before the practice questions.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Formation of Ions
topics.description: The process by which atoms lose or gain electrons to form ions, and how this relates to achieving a stable, full outer electron shell.
learning_objectives: Explain the process of ion formation via electron loss or gain
Predict the charge of an ion formed by a main group element
Relate ion formation to achieving noble gas electron configuration
topics.explanation: Ions form when atoms lose or gain electrons in order to achieve a more stable, lower-energy electron arrangement, most commonly a full outer shell matching the electron configuration of the nearest noble gas. Metal atoms, having relatively few valence electrons, typically lose electrons to form positive ions (cations); the number of electrons lost usually matches the number of valence electrons, so that the resulting ion has the same electron configuration as the noble gas before it in the periodic table. Non-metal atoms, having relatively many valence electrons, typically gain electrons to form negative ions (anions); the number of electrons gained is usually enough to complete the outer shell to 8 electrons (or 2, for elements near helium), giving the resulting ion the same electron configuration as the noble gas after it in the periodic table.
key_concepts: Electron loss forms cations; electron gain forms anions
Predicting ion charge from group number

worked_examples.problem: Predict the ion formed by an aluminium atom (electron configuration 2,8,3), and explain your reasoning.
worked_examples.working: Aluminium has 3 valence electrons. Losing all 3 gives a full outer shell matching neon's configuration (2,8).
worked_examples.answer: Aluminium forms Al3+, by losing its 3 valence electrons to achieve a stable, full outer shell (2,8).

practical_applications: Predicting ion formation is fundamental to predicting compound formulae and the properties of ionic compounds used throughout industry
common_mistakes: Forgetting to check whether an element is closer to losing few electrons (as a metal) or gaining few electrons (as a non-metal) to reach a full shell — always identify the shortest route to a stable configuration
misconceptions: Believing all atoms gain electrons to complete a full outer shell — metals more easily lose their few valence electrons to expose a full shell underneath, rather than gaining many electrons to fill their outer shell completely
tips: For groups 1-3, predict ion charge = group number (positive); for groups 15-17, predict ion charge = group number − 8 (negative)

basic.question: State the ion formed by a sodium atom.
State the ion formed by a fluorine atom.

intermediate.question: Explain why a sulfur atom (2,8,6) is more likely to gain 2 electrons than to lose 6 electrons when forming an ion.
intermediate.answer: Gaining 2 electrons only requires overcoming the energy cost of adding 2 electrons to reach a full outer shell of 8 (2,8,8), whereas losing 6 electrons would require removing electrons from a full, stable inner shell, needing vastly more energy. Gaining 2 electrons is by far the more energetically favourable route to a stable, full outer shell, so sulfur forms S2− rather than a highly charged positive ion.

advanced.question: Explain why elements in the middle of a period (such as carbon, Group 14) do not readily form simple ions, unlike elements at either end of a period.
advanced.answer: Carbon has 4 valence electrons, meaning it would need to either lose 4 electrons (forming a 4+ ion) or gain 4 electrons (forming a 4− ion) to achieve a stable, full outer shell. Both processes require a very large amount of energy, since losing multiple electrons against increasing positive charge, or gaining multiple electrons against increasing negative charge/repulsion, is energetically very costly. This makes forming a simple ion energetically unfavourable for carbon (and similar Group 14 elements), so these elements typically form covalent bonds by sharing electrons instead, which is a much less energy-intensive way of achieving a stable outer shell.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why magnesium forms a 2+ ion, using ideas about electron configuration and stability.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Magnesium has the electron configuration 2,8,2, with 2 valence electrons (1 mark). Losing these 2 electrons gives magnesium a full outer shell identical to the noble gas neon (2,8), a stable, low-energy arrangement, so magnesium consistently forms a 2+ ion (1 mark).

topics.summary: Ions form as atoms lose or gain electrons to achieve a stable, full outer shell matching the nearest noble gas configuration. Metals typically lose their few valence electrons (forming cations); non-metals typically gain a small number of electrons (forming anions).
revision_notes: Ions form to achieve noble gas configuration (full outer shell)
Metals: lose electrons (few valence electrons) → cations
Non-metals: gain electrons (many valence electrons) → anions
Middle-period elements (e.g. carbon) don't readily form simple ions — too energetically costly

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Ionic Lattice Structures
topics.description: The regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of oppositely charged ions in an ionic compound, and the concept of lattice energy.
learning_objectives: Describe the structure of a giant ionic lattice
Explain how coordination number relates to ion size and charge
Define lattice energy and relate it to ionic compound stability
topics.explanation: Ionic compounds exist as giant ionic lattices: a regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of positive and negative ions, extending throughout the solid, held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction acting in all directions. Each ion is surrounded by a specific number of oppositely charged neighbouring ions, called its coordination number, which depends on the relative sizes of the ions involved (for sodium chloride, each ion has a coordination number of 6, arranged in a face-centred cubic-type structure). Lattice energy (or lattice enthalpy) is the energy released when one mole of an ionic solid forms from its constituent gaseous ions; it is a measure of the strength of the ionic bonding throughout the lattice, and depends on the charges of the ions involved (higher charges give stronger attraction, more exothermic lattice energy) and the distance between ion centres (smaller ions allow closer approach and stronger attraction, more exothermic lattice energy).
key_concepts: Lattice energy: definition and factors affecting it (charge, ionic radius)

definitions.definition: A regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of positive and negative ions extending throughout an ionic solid.
The number of oppositely charged ions immediately surrounding a given ion in a lattice structure.
The energy released when one mole of an ionic solid forms from its constituent ions in the gaseous state; a measure of ionic bond strength within the lattice.

equations: Na+(g) + Cl−(g) → NaCl(s)  (lattice energy formation equation)

worked_examples.problem: Predict whether magnesium oxide (Mg2+, O2−) or sodium chloride (Na+, Cl−) has the more exothermic (larger magnitude) lattice energy, and explain why.
worked_examples.working: Compare ionic charges: Mg2+/O2− ions both carry a charge of 2, while Na+/Cl− ions each carry a charge of 1. Greater ionic charge increases electrostatic attraction.
worked_examples.answer: Magnesium oxide has the more exothermic lattice energy, since its 2+ and 2− ions attract each other far more strongly than the 1+ and 1− ions in sodium chloride, due to the greater ionic charges involved.

practical_applications: Lattice energy trends help explain and predict the melting points, solubility and thermal stability of different ionic compounds, relevant to material selection in industry
laboratory_applications: Comparing melting points of different ionic compounds as indirect experimental evidence for relative lattice energy/bond strength
common_mistakes: Confusing lattice energy (ions coming together to form a solid, always exothermic) with the reverse process, sometimes called lattice dissociation enthalpy (breaking a solid apart into gaseous ions, always endothermic) — always check which direction the question specifies
misconceptions: Believing coordination number is always the same for every ionic compound — it varies depending on the relative sizes of the cation and anion involved, giving different lattice structures for different compounds
tips: Remember the two key factors for comparing lattice energy: greater ionic charge = more exothermic (stronger); smaller ionic radius = more exothermic (stronger), since ions can approach more closely

basic.question: State the coordination number of each ion in the sodium chloride lattice.
Define lattice energy.
basic.answer: The energy released when one mole of an ionic solid forms from its constituent ions in the gaseous state.

intermediate.question: Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
intermediate.answer: Magnesium oxide contains Mg2+ and O2− ions, both with a charge of 2, giving much stronger electrostatic attraction (and therefore a more exothermic, larger-magnitude lattice energy) than the 1+ and 1− ions in sodium chloride. This stronger ionic bonding throughout the magnesium oxide lattice requires more energy to overcome, giving it a considerably higher melting point than sodium chloride.

advanced.question: Explain why lithium fluoride has a more exothermic lattice energy than sodium chloride, considering both ions have the same charges (1+ and 1−).
advanced.answer: Although both compounds involve ions with the same charges (1+ and 1−), lithium and fluoride ions are both smaller than sodium and chloride ions respectively (lithium and fluoride being higher up their respective groups, with smaller atomic and ionic radii). Smaller ions can approach more closely to one another in the lattice, and since electrostatic attraction increases as the distance between charges decreases, the closer approach possible in lithium fluoride results in stronger electrostatic attraction and a more exothermic (more negative) lattice energy than in sodium chloride.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain, using ionic charge and ionic radius, why calcium oxide has a more exothermic lattice energy than potassium chloride.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Calcium oxide contains Ca2+ and O2− ions, each with a charge of 2, while potassium chloride contains K+ and Cl− ions, each with a charge of only 1; greater ionic charge increases electrostatic attraction (1 mark). Additionally, calcium and oxide ions are generally smaller than potassium and chloride ions, allowing closer approach between ions (1 mark). Both the greater charge and smaller ionic radii in calcium oxide result in stronger electrostatic attraction throughout the lattice, giving calcium oxide a more exothermic lattice energy than potassium chloride (1 mark).

topics.summary: Ionic compounds form giant lattices with a regular, repeating structure and a specific coordination number determined by relative ion sizes. Lattice energy measures the strength of this ionic bonding, becoming more exothermic with greater ionic charge and smaller ionic radius.
revision_notes: Giant ionic lattice: regular, repeating 3D structure
Coordination number depends on relative ion sizes
Lattice energy: exothermic; increases (more negative) with greater charge, smaller radius
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: 3D giant ionic lattice structure of sodium chloride showing alternating Na+ and Cl- ions]

images.description: A grid of alternating orange Na+ and teal Cl- circles arranged in a repeating checkerboard pattern representing the giant ionic lattice, with a labelled legend distinguishing the two ion types and a caption noting each ion is surrounded by six oppositely charged neighbours.
images.purpose: Gives students a concrete visual of the 'giant, repeating structure' concept that is otherwise abstract from text description alone, directly supporting the coordination number discussion.
images.placement: After the main explanation paragraph, before the key concepts list.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Properties of Ionic Compounds
topics.description: The characteristic physical properties of ionic compounds — high melting points, brittleness, and electrical conductivity only when molten or dissolved — explained by their giant lattice structure.
learning_objectives: State the typical physical properties of ionic compounds
Explain these properties in terms of ionic lattice structure and bonding
Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or in aqueous solution
topics.explanation: Ionic compounds typically show several characteristic physical properties, all explained by their giant lattice structure and strong electrostatic bonding. They have high melting and boiling points, because a large number of strong ionic bonds throughout the lattice must be overcome to separate the ions, requiring a great deal of energy. They are hard but brittle: applying force can shift a layer of ions so that ions of the same charge become aligned next to each other; the resulting strong repulsion between like-charged ions causes the lattice to shatter along that plane. Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity when solid, because the ions are held in fixed positions within the lattice and cannot move to carry charge; however, they do conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions are then free to move and carry charge through the liquid. Many ionic compounds are soluble in water, since polar water molecules can surround and separate the individual ions (see Solubility of Ionic Compounds).
key_concepts: Hard but brittle (like-ion repulsion on shifting)
Conduct electricity only when molten/dissolved (mobile ions)
practical_applications: Ionic compounds' electrical behaviour when molten is exploited in electrolysis (e.g. extraction of aluminium); their high melting points make some ionic compounds useful as refractory materials
laboratory_applications: Testing electrical conductivity of a solid ionic compound, then repeating when molten or dissolved, to demonstrate the role of mobile ions
common_mistakes: Believing ionic compounds never conduct electricity — they simply do not conduct as solids, but do conduct when molten or in aqueous solution, since the ions become free to move
misconceptions: Believing ionic compounds are brittle because the bonds are 'weak' — the bonds are actually very strong (giving high melting points); brittleness arises from the specific way the rigid lattice responds to force (layers shifting, causing repulsion between like-charged ions), not from weak bonding
tips: Always link each property back to the underlying structure: strong bonds throughout the lattice explain high melting point; fixed ion positions in a solid explain lack of conductivity when solid; freely moving ions when molten/dissolved explain conductivity in those states

basic.question: State whether solid ionic compounds conduct electricity.
basic.answer: No, they do not conduct electricity as solids.

basic.question: State one typical physical property of ionic compounds.
basic.answer: Any one of: high melting/boiling point, hard but brittle, conducts electricity when molten/dissolved, often soluble in water.

intermediate.question: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.
intermediate.answer: Ionic compounds consist of a giant lattice held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between many oppositely charged ions throughout the structure. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these numerous strong ionic bonds and separate the ions, giving ionic compounds high melting points.

intermediate.question: Explain why ionic compounds are brittle, even though the ionic bonding is very strong.
intermediate.answer: When sufficient force is applied to an ionic lattice, a layer of ions can be shifted slightly relative to the layer beneath it. This shift can bring ions of the same charge into close alignment with one another, and the resulting strong repulsion between these like-charged ions causes the lattice to fracture or shatter along that plane, making ionic compounds brittle despite their strong overall bonding.

advanced.question: Explain why molten lead bromide conducts electricity, while solid lead bromide does not, and describe what happens at each electrode during electrolysis of molten lead bromide.
advanced.answer: In solid lead bromide, the Pb2+ and Br− ions are held in fixed positions within the rigid ionic lattice and cannot move freely, so no charge can be carried through the solid. When melted, the rigid lattice structure breaks down and the ions become free to move throughout the liquid, allowing them to carry electric charge, so molten lead bromide conducts electricity. During electrolysis of molten lead bromide, positive Pb2+ ions migrate to the negative electrode (cathode), where they gain electrons and are reduced to form liquid lead metal; negative Br− ions migrate to the positive electrode (anode), where they lose electrons and are oxidised to form bromine gas/liquid.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: In solid sodium chloride, the Na+ and Cl− ions are held in fixed positions within the rigid giant ionic lattice and are not free to move (1 mark), so they cannot carry electric charge through the solid (1 mark). When molten, the lattice structure breaks down and the ions become free to move, allowing them to carry electric charge, so molten sodium chloride conducts electricity (1 mark).

topics.summary: Ionic compounds have high melting points (many strong bonds to overcome), are hard but brittle (like-ion repulsion when layers shift), and conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved (mobile ions), all explained by their giant lattice structure.
revision_notes: High melting point: many strong ionic bonds throughout lattice
Brittle: layers shift → like-charge repulsion → shatters
Conducts only when molten/dissolved: ions become mobile
Often soluble in water

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Covalent Bonding
topics.description: The sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two non-metal atoms, forming a strong directional bond.
learning_objectives: Define covalent bonding
Explain why sharing electrons leads to a stable arrangement for both atoms
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for simple covalently bonded molecules
topics.explanation: Covalent bonding is the sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two atoms, typically both non-metals. Each shared pair of electrons counts towards the outer shell of both atoms involved, allowing both to achieve a stable, full outer shell (usually 8 electrons, or 2 for hydrogen) without either atom needing to fully lose or gain electrons outright. The shared pair of electrons is attracted to both positively charged nuclei simultaneously, and it is this mutual attraction that holds the two atoms together as a covalent bond. Covalent bonds are directional (acting specifically between the two bonded atoms, unlike the non-directional attraction in ionic bonding) and can involve one shared pair (single bond), two shared pairs (double bond), or three shared pairs (triple bond) between the same two atoms.
key_concepts: Both atoms achieve stable outer shell
Directional bond (mutual attraction of nuclei to shared electrons)
Single, double and triple bonds possible

definitions.definition: A strong bond formed by the sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two atoms.

worked_examples.problem: Describe the covalent bonding in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl.
worked_examples.working: Hydrogen (1 electron) needs 1 more electron for a full shell (2). Chlorine (2,8,7) needs 1 more electron for a full outer shell (2,8,8). Both atoms share one pair of electrons.
worked_examples.answer: Hydrogen and chlorine share one pair of electrons (a single covalent bond), with hydrogen achieving a full shell of 2 electrons and chlorine achieving a full outer shell of 8 electrons.

practical_applications: Covalent bonding underlies the structure of the vast majority of biological molecules (proteins, DNA, carbohydrates) and organic compounds central to the chemical industry
common_mistakes: Drawing dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent molecules that show complete electron transfer (as in ionic bonding) rather than shared pairs of electrons
misconceptions: Believing only non-metals bonded to different non-metals can form covalent bonds — covalent bonding also occurs between atoms of the same non-metal element, e.g. in O2, N2, Cl2
tips: In a dot-and-cross diagram, a shared pair of electrons is shown as one dot and one cross drawn together in the overlapping region between the two atoms

basic.question: Define covalent bonding.
basic.answer: The sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two atoms.

basic.question: State the type of atoms typically involved in covalent bonding.

intermediate.question: Explain why a molecule of water, H2O, contains two covalent bonds.
intermediate.answer: Oxygen (2,6) needs 2 more electrons to achieve a full outer shell of 8, so it forms a covalent bond with each of two separate hydrogen atoms, sharing one pair of electrons with each; each hydrogen atom then has a full shell of 2 electrons, and oxygen has a full outer shell of 8 electrons (2 from each of the two shared pairs, plus its own remaining 4 outer electrons).

advanced.question: Explain why covalent bonds are described as 'directional', unlike ionic bonds.
advanced.answer: A covalent bond arises from a specific, localised pair of electrons shared between two particular atoms, concentrated in the region of space directly between their two nuclei; the resulting attraction is therefore specific to that particular bond direction and pair of atoms. Ionic bonding, in contrast, arises from the general electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, which acts equally in all directions around each ion (non-directional), attracting any oppositely charged ion nearby rather than being localised to one specific bond.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain how covalent bonding allows two chlorine atoms to both achieve a full outer shell in a Cl2 molecule.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Each chlorine atom has 7 valence electrons and needs 1 more electron to complete its outer shell (1 mark). The two chlorine atoms share one pair of electrons between them, forming a single covalent bond (1 mark). This shared pair counts towards the outer shell of both atoms, so each chlorine atom effectively has a full outer shell of 8 electrons (its own 6 non-bonding electrons plus the shared pair) (1 mark).

topics.summary: Covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between (typically non-metal) atoms, allowing both to achieve a stable, full outer shell. The shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei, forming a strong, directional bond, which can be single, double or triple depending on the number of shared pairs.
revision_notes: Covalent bond: shared pair(s) of electrons, both atoms reach full shell
Directional (localised between two specific atoms)
Can be single, double or triple bond

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Single Covalent Bonds
topics.description: A covalent bond formed by sharing one pair of electrons between two atoms, the most common and typically weakest/longest type of covalent bond.
learning_objectives: Define a single covalent bond
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for molecules containing single bonds
Compare single bonds to double and triple bonds in terms of length and strength
topics.explanation: A single covalent bond consists of one shared pair of electrons between two atoms. It is the most common type of covalent bond, found in molecules such as H2, Cl2, HCl, H2O, CH4 and countless organic compounds. Compared to double and triple bonds between the same two types of atom, a single bond is generally the longest and weakest, since fewer shared electrons means less overall electron density holding the two nuclei together, and therefore a somewhat greater equilibrium distance between the bonded nuclei and a lower bond energy required to break it.
key_concepts: Longest and weakest compared to double/triple bonds between the same atoms

definitions.definition: A covalent bond formed by the sharing of one pair of electrons between two atoms.

worked_examples.problem: State the number of single covalent bonds in a molecule of methane, CH4.
worked_examples.working: Carbon (4 valence electrons) forms one covalent bond with each of 4 separate hydrogen atoms.
worked_examples.answer: 4 single covalent bonds (one C-H bond to each hydrogen atom).

practical_applications: Single covalent C-C and C-H bonds form the structural backbone of the vast majority of organic molecules, including fuels, plastics and biological macromolecules
common_mistakes: Assuming a single line in a structural formula (e.g. C-C) always represents the same bond strength regardless of which atoms are involved — bond strength depends on both the number of shared pairs and which specific elements are bonded
misconceptions: Believing 'single' bond means a weak or unimportant bond — single covalent bonds are still strong, directional bonds, simply weaker than a double or triple bond between the same two types of atom
tips: A single line in a structural formula (e.g. H-H, C-H) represents a single covalent bond, one shared pair of electrons

basic.question: State the number of shared electron pairs in a single covalent bond.
Name a diatomic molecule containing a single covalent bond.
basic.answer: Any one of: H2, Cl2, HCl (or similar).

intermediate.question: Explain why a single C-C bond is longer than a double C=C bond.
intermediate.answer: A single bond involves only one shared pair of electrons between the two carbon atoms, providing less overall electron density (and therefore less attractive force) holding the nuclei together compared to a double bond, which involves two shared pairs. With less attractive force pulling the nuclei together, the equilibrium distance between the two carbon nuclei is greater in a single bond, making it longer than a double bond.

advanced.question: Explain, in terms of bond energy, why single C-C bonds in alkanes are generally less reactive towards addition reactions than the double C=C bonds in alkenes.
advanced.answer: A single C-C bond consists of one sigma (σ) bond, formed by direct, end-on overlap of orbitals, which is relatively strong and unreactive on its own. A double C=C bond consists of one sigma bond plus an additional pi (π) bond, formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the bond axis; this pi bond has electron density less directly between the two nuclei and is more exposed/accessible to attack by other reagents, and is generally weaker and more easily broken than a sigma bond. This makes the double bond, and its associated pi bond specifically, much more reactive towards addition reactions (where the pi bond breaks and new sigma bonds form) than the single C-C bonds found throughout alkanes, which generally only undergo substitution reactions requiring more forcing conditions.

exam_style_questions.question: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram (describe in words) for a molecule of hydrogen, H2, and state the number of shared electron pairs.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Each hydrogen atom contributes one electron to a single shared pair positioned in the overlapping region between the two hydrogen nuclei, giving both hydrogen atoms a full outer shell of 2 electrons (1 mark). This represents one shared pair of electrons: a single covalent bond (1 mark).

topics.summary: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons between two atoms — the most common covalent bond type, generally longer and weaker than a double or triple bond between the same two atoms.
revision_notes: Single bond: 1 shared electron pair
Most common bond type; forms backbone of organic molecules
Longer, weaker than double/triple bond (same atoms)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Double Covalent Bonds
topics.description: A covalent bond formed by sharing two pairs of electrons between two atoms, shorter and stronger than a single bond.
learning_objectives: Define a double covalent bond
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for molecules containing double bonds
Describe the sigma and pi bond composition of a double bond
topics.explanation: A double covalent bond consists of two shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms, found in molecules such as O2 and CO2, and in the C=C and C=O functional groups central to organic chemistry (alkenes, carbonyl compounds). A double bond is shorter and stronger than a single bond between the same two types of atom, since the greater electron density between the two nuclei results in stronger overall attraction and a shorter equilibrium bond length. At a more detailed level, a double bond consists of one sigma (σ) bond, formed by direct, end-on overlap of orbitals along the axis between the two nuclei, plus one pi (π) bond, formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below this axis; the pi bond restricts rotation around the double bond, which is important in explaining geometric (cis-trans) isomerism.
key_concepts: Shorter and stronger than single bond
Composed of one sigma and one pi bond

definitions.definition: A covalent bond formed by the sharing of two pairs of electrons between two atoms, composed of one sigma and one pi bond.
A covalent bond formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals, found in double and triple bonds in addition to a sigma bond.

worked_examples.problem: State the number of shared electron pairs in the C=O double bond of carbon dioxide, and describe its bond composition.
worked_examples.working: A double bond, by definition, involves two shared pairs of electrons.
worked_examples.answer: 2 shared electron pairs, composed of one sigma bond (direct overlap) and one pi bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals).

practical_applications: The C=C double bond in alkenes and the C=O double bond in carbonyl compounds are central to organic synthesis, polymer chemistry, and countless industrial processes
laboratory_applications: Testing for the presence of a C=C double bond using bromine water, which decolourises rapidly in the presence of alkenes due to an addition reaction across the double bond
common_mistakes: Assuming a double bond is simply 'two single bonds side by side' — it consists of one sigma bond and one distinctly different pi bond, which behave differently (the pi bond being generally weaker and more reactive)
misconceptions: Believing free rotation is possible around a double bond, as it is around a single bond — the pi bond component of a double bond restricts rotation, since rotating the bond would require breaking the sideways p orbital overlap, which is energetically costly at normal temperatures
tips: Remember: a double bond = 1 sigma + 1 pi bond; this pi bond is what restricts rotation and is chemically more reactive than the sigma bond component

basic.question: State the number of shared electron pairs in a double covalent bond.
Name the two types of individual bond that together make up a double covalent bond.
basic.answer: One sigma (σ) bond and one pi (π) bond.

intermediate.question: Explain why a C=C double bond is shorter than a C-C single bond.
intermediate.answer: A double bond has two shared pairs of electrons (greater electron density) between the two carbon nuclei, compared to only one shared pair in a single bond. This greater electron density results in a stronger overall attractive force pulling the two nuclei together, resulting in a shorter equilibrium bond length for the double bond compared to the single bond.

advanced.question: Explain why rotation is restricted around a C=C double bond but not around a C-C single bond, and state one consequence of this for isomerism.
advanced.answer: A double bond consists of a sigma bond (direct, end-on orbital overlap, allowing free rotation around its axis without breaking the bond) plus a pi bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the bond axis). Rotating one part of the molecule relative to the other around a double bond would require the p orbitals forming the pi bond to twist out of alignment, breaking this sideways overlap and therefore breaking the pi bond, which requires significant energy and does not happen freely at normal temperatures. A single bond, having only a sigma bond, can rotate freely without breaking any bond. This restricted rotation around double bonds is the reason geometric (cis-trans) isomerism can exist for suitably substituted alkenes, since the relative positions of substituent groups around the double bond are fixed rather than freely interconvertible.

exam_style_questions.question: Describe the composition of a double covalent bond in terms of sigma and pi bonds, and explain why this makes double bonds more reactive than single bonds towards addition reactions.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: A double bond consists of one sigma bond (direct, end-on orbital overlap) and one pi bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals, with electron density above and below the bond axis) (1 mark). The pi bond's electron density is less directly shielded between the nuclei and is more exposed/accessible than the sigma bond, making it relatively weaker and easier to break (1 mark). This makes the pi bond component of a double bond particularly susceptible to attack by other reagents, explaining why molecules with double bonds readily undergo addition reactions, where the pi bond breaks to form two new sigma bonds (1 mark).

topics.summary: A double covalent bond involves two shared electron pairs, composed of one sigma and one pi bond, making it shorter and stronger than a single bond but with restricted rotation and greater reactivity due to the more exposed pi bond.
revision_notes: Double bond: 2 shared electron pairs = 1 sigma + 1 pi bond
Shorter, stronger than single bond
Restricted rotation (pi bond) → enables cis-trans isomerism
Pi bond is more reactive (addition reactions)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Triple Covalent Bonds
topics.description: A covalent bond formed by sharing three pairs of electrons between two atoms, the shortest and strongest type of covalent bond, as seen in N2.
learning_objectives: Define a triple covalent bond
Describe the sigma and pi bond composition of a triple bond
Explain why triple bonds make molecules such as N2 particularly unreactive
topics.explanation: A triple covalent bond consists of three shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms, found notably in the nitrogen molecule, N2, and in the carbon-carbon triple bond of alkynes (e.g. ethyne, C2H2). A triple bond is the shortest and strongest type of covalent bond between two given atoms, since it involves the greatest electron density between the two nuclei, resulting in the strongest overall attractive force and shortest equilibrium bond length. A triple bond is composed of one sigma (σ) bond plus two pi (π) bonds (formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals in two different perpendicular planes). The very high bond energy of the triple bond in N2 (one of the strongest known covalent bonds) is the reason nitrogen gas is so chemically unreactive at room temperature, despite reactions involving nitrogen (such as in the Haber process) often being thermodynamically favourable overall.
key_concepts: Shortest and strongest covalent bond type
Composed of one sigma and two pi bonds

definitions.definition: A covalent bond formed by the sharing of three pairs of electrons between two atoms, composed of one sigma and two pi bonds.

worked_examples.problem: Explain why N2 requires a very high activation energy to react, referring to its bonding.
worked_examples.working: N2 contains a triple covalent bond between the two nitrogen atoms.
worked_examples.answer: The triple bond in N2 has a very high bond energy (it is one of the strongest known covalent bonds), so breaking it to allow nitrogen to react requires a large amount of activation energy, making N2 kinetically very unreactive under normal conditions.

practical_applications: The strength of the N2 triple bond is central to why the Haber process requires high pressure, a catalyst, and moderately high temperature to achieve a viable rate of ammonia production
common_mistakes: Assuming a triple bond is simply three times as strong as a single bond in a straightforward numerical sense — while it is considerably stronger, the relationship is not a simple threefold multiplication, since sigma and pi bonds have different individual strengths
misconceptions: Believing N2's lack of reactivity means reactions to form nitrogen compounds are thermodynamically unfavourable — many nitrogen-fixation reactions (e.g. the Haber process) are thermodynamically favourable (exothermic) overall; N2's unreactivity is a kinetic barrier (high activation energy from the strong triple bond) rather than a thermodynamic one
tips: Remember: triple bond = 1 sigma + 2 pi bonds; this is the origin of both its shortness/strength and its role in explaining N2's kinetic stability

basic.question: State the number of shared electron pairs in a triple covalent bond.
Name a diatomic molecule containing a triple covalent bond.

intermediate.question: Describe the composition of a triple covalent bond in terms of sigma and pi bonds.
intermediate.answer: A triple bond consists of one sigma bond (direct, end-on orbital overlap along the axis between the two nuclei) and two pi bonds (formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals in two different perpendicular planes around the bond axis).

intermediate.question: Explain why a triple bond is shorter than a double bond between the same two atoms.
intermediate.answer: A triple bond has three shared pairs of electrons, giving greater overall electron density between the two nuclei compared to a double bond's two shared pairs. This greater electron density results in stronger overall attraction pulling the nuclei together, giving the triple bond a shorter equilibrium bond length than the double bond.

advanced.question: Explain why nitrogen gas is described as kinetically stable but not necessarily thermodynamically stable with respect to forming compounds such as ammonia.
advanced.answer: Kinetic stability refers to the rate at which a reaction proceeds, governed by the activation energy required; N2's very strong triple bond gives it a very high activation energy for most reactions, meaning reactions involving N2 proceed extremely slowly (or not at all) under normal conditions, making it kinetically stable/unreactive. Thermodynamic stability refers to whether a reaction is energetically favourable overall (exothermic, releasing energy); many reactions of nitrogen, such as its combination with hydrogen to form ammonia in the Haber process, are in fact exothermic and thermodynamically favourable. This distinction explains why, despite nitrogen's compounds often being more thermodynamically stable than N2 itself, N2 persists largely unreacted in the atmosphere without special conditions (high temperature, pressure, and a catalyst, as used industrially) to overcome its high activation energy.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why the Haber process requires a catalyst and relatively high temperature, referring to the bonding in nitrogen gas.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Nitrogen gas contains a very strong triple covalent bond between its two nitrogen atoms, giving the molecule a very high bond energy and therefore a high activation energy for reactions (1 mark). A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, allowing the triple bond to be broken more readily (1 mark). A relatively high temperature provides additional energy to the reacting particles, increasing the proportion with enough energy to react successfully and achieving a commercially viable reaction rate, despite the strength of the N2 triple bond (1 mark).

topics.summary: A triple covalent bond has three shared electron pairs (one sigma, two pi bonds), making it the shortest and strongest type of covalent bond. The exceptionally strong triple bond in N2 explains nitrogen's kinetic unreactivity, despite many of its reactions being thermodynamically favourable.
revision_notes: Triple bond: 3 shared electron pairs = 1 sigma + 2 pi bonds
Shortest, strongest covalent bond type
N2's triple bond: very high bond energy → kinetically unreactive (high activation energy)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Coordinate (Dative) Covalent Bonds
topics.description: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons originate from the same atom, as seen in the formation of the ammonium ion and in some complex ions.
learning_objectives: Define a coordinate (dative) covalent bond
Describe the formation of the ammonium ion as an example
Represent dative bonds using an arrow notation in displayed formulae
topics.explanation: A coordinate covalent bond, also called a dative covalent bond, is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom (the 'donor'), rather than one electron from each atom as in an ordinary covalent bond; the other atom or ion involved (the 'acceptor') provides an empty orbital to receive this donated electron pair. A classic example is the formation of the ammonium ion, NH4+: the nitrogen atom in ammonia (NH3) has a lone pair of electrons, which it donates entirely to a hydrogen ion (H+, which has no electrons of its own and an empty 1s orbital), forming a fourth N-H bond. Once formed, a dative covalent bond is identical in every measurable way to an ordinary covalent bond (the same length and strength); the distinction only concerns its origin (both electrons from one atom, rather than one from each), and is often shown as an arrow (from donor to acceptor) rather than a line in displayed formulae, at least for the bond as it initially forms.
key_concepts: Both electrons donated by one atom
Identical to ordinary covalent bond once formed

definitions.definition: A covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are provided by the same atom, rather than one from each bonding atom.

worked_examples.problem: Explain how a dative covalent bond forms between ammonia and a hydrogen ion to produce the ammonium ion.
worked_examples.working: Ammonia's nitrogen atom has a lone (non-bonding) pair of electrons. A hydrogen ion, H+, has no electrons and an empty orbital.
worked_examples.answer: The lone pair of electrons on nitrogen is donated entirely into the empty orbital of the H+ ion, forming a new N-H bond in which both electrons originated from nitrogen; this produces the ammonium ion, NH4+, with an overall 1+ charge.

practical_applications: Dative covalent bonding is essential to understanding the structure and stability of many complex ions formed by transition metals with ligands, relevant to catalysis and coordination chemistry
common_mistakes: Assuming a dative bond is weaker or somehow different in strength from an ordinary covalent bond once formed — it is identical in length and strength; only its origin (both electrons from one atom) differs
misconceptions: Believing all four N-H bonds in NH4+ remain distinguishable from one another after formation — once the dative bond has formed, all four N-H bonds in the ammonium ion become completely identical and indistinguishable, since electrons are not 'labelled' by their original source
tips: Look for a lone pair of electrons on one species (the donor) and an empty orbital or missing electron on the other (the acceptor, often a positively charged ion like H+) as the key indicator that a dative bond is about to form

basic.question: Define a coordinate (dative) covalent bond.
basic.answer: A covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are provided by the same atom.

basic.question: Name the ion formed when ammonia reacts with a hydrogen ion via dative covalent bonding.

intermediate.question: Explain why a hydrogen ion, H+, is able to accept a lone pair of electrons from ammonia to form a dative bond.
intermediate.answer: A hydrogen ion, H+, has lost its only electron and therefore has an empty 1s orbital with no electrons of its own. This empty orbital can accept the lone pair of electrons donated by the nitrogen atom in ammonia, forming a new covalent bond in which both electrons originate from nitrogen.

advanced.question: Explain why, despite forming via a different mechanism, the N-H bond formed by dative bonding in NH4+ is indistinguishable from the other three N-H bonds in the ion.
advanced.answer: Once a dative covalent bond has formed, the shared pair of electrons is delocalised across the bond in exactly the same way as in an ordinary covalent bond; there is no physical 'marker' distinguishing which atom the electrons originally came from. Since all four N-H bonds in NH4+ involve identical atoms (N and H) with an identical shared electron pair arrangement and the same surrounding electronic and structural environment (due to the symmetric, tetrahedral shape of the ion, see VSEPR Theory), all four bonds become completely equivalent in length, strength and character, making the bond formed by the original dative donation indistinguishable from the other three ordinary covalent N-H bonds.

exam_style_questions.question: Describe how a dative covalent bond differs from an ordinary covalent bond in terms of its formation, and explain why the two types of bond are indistinguishable once formed.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: In an ordinary covalent bond, each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair; in a dative covalent bond, both electrons of the shared pair are provided by a single atom (the donor), while the other atom (the acceptor) provides an empty orbital (1 mark). Once formed, the shared electron pair behaves identically regardless of its origin, since there is no physical difference between an electron that came from the donor atom and one that would have come from the acceptor in an ordinary bond (1 mark); the bond has the same length, strength and behaviour as any other covalent bond of the same type, so the two are indistinguishable once formed (1 mark).

topics.summary: A coordinate (dative) covalent bond forms when both shared electrons come from a single donor atom with a lone pair, accepted into an empty orbital of another atom or ion (e.g. NH3 donating to H+ to form NH4+). Once formed, it is identical to an ordinary covalent bond.
revision_notes: Dative bond: both electrons from ONE atom (donor); other atom (acceptor) has empty orbital
Classic example: NH3 + H+ → NH4+
Shown with an arrow (donor → acceptor) in displayed formulae
Identical to ordinary covalent bond once formed
